sections.h2: Who handles your Victoria property tax
sections.html:
A Victoria bill comes out of three offices. The Victoria Central Appraisal District appraises the house, sends you the value notice, hears protests and runs the exemption program. Each taxing unit votes on its own rate. After that, the Victoria County Tax Office is the one that issues the statement and takes your payment.

Within city limits, expect the one bill to list county, school and city charges, with junior college, hospital or road district lines in some cases.

  • Questions on value, exemptions, names or addresses: Victoria Central Appraisal District, 2805 N. Navarro St., Suite 300, phone (361) 576-3621, open weekdays from 8:00 AM until 5:00 PM.
  • Bill, payment or penalty questions go to the Victoria County Tax Office, 205 N. Bridge St., Suite 101, phone (361) 576-3671.
  • City rate and budget questions: the City of Victoria.

Victoria is home to about 66,500 people, with moderately priced housing: a $207,100 median value and $1,172 median rent. Owners live in 57.9% of the homes. Since values are modest, the flat school exemption covers a large part of what the school district would tax.

In 2025 the city rate was $0.4790 per $100 of taxable value; for 2026 it proposed $0.4538. Treat your own statement as the final word.

The council's 2026 choice sits between two benchmarks, $0.4538 (no-new-revenue) and $0.4652 (voter-approval).

Those numbers are only the city's portion. For the full rate on your account, ask the tax office.

October brings the statement from the county tax office, due on arrival. Because nothing is late until February 1, plan around January 31.

Penalty begins at 6% and goes up a point on the first of every month after that, then gains 2 points on July 1 to reach 12%. Interest is its own charge at 1% monthly. A check mailed at the end of January counts only with a postmark of January 31 or earlier. An account still open in July may also draw up to 20 percent for a collection attorney.

The certified roll reaches the tax office from the appraisal district by July 25. The office matches it to each unit's adopted rate and builds the October statements. Value notices come in mid-April, and units set rates during August and September.

  • Still no bill on November 1? The tax office can send a copy. Lost mail does not erase the tax or release the lien.
  • With an escrow account, the lender normally pays the bill. If a statement reaches you anyway, add your loan number and forward it.
  • Lenders have to ask the county for their clients' statements by late August, or the owner may get the bill directly.

There are two ways to cut the bill. One is a residence homestead exemption. The other is a protest, if your value notice looks too high. Both go through the appraisal district, never the tax office.

The general exemption requires that the house be your main home on January 1. Owners 65 and older receive another exemption, and there are separate exemptions for disabled homeowners and for a disabled veteran or a veteran's surviving spouse. Texas school districts all grant $140,000 on a homestead, and seniors and disabled owners get $60,000 more. Taxing units may also adopt a percentage exemption, so find out which ones the Victoria units have.

Under House Bill 585 an applicant must supply:

  • A Texas driver license or ID card copy, where the address on the license, vehicle registration or a utility bill matches the property.
  • A sworn statement that you claim no other homestead, in Texas or elsewhere.
  • For a manufactured home, the ownership and location statement from the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs.

Military members on active duty, and their spouses, can ask the chief appraiser to waive the address match. Reapplying every year is unnecessary unless the chief appraiser requests it. The district's Forms page has the paperwork, and finished forms can be emailed to exemptions@victoriacad.org.

Homesteads also have a state cap of 10% a year on appraised value growth after your first qualifying year is behind you. For seniors and disabled owners, the school tax freeze carries over to a replacement Texas homestead.

Your notice of protest must reach the appraisal district by May 15, or within 30 days after your value notice arrives, whichever is later. The district's taxpayer page links Form 50-132 and a guide to filling it out, plus a Comptroller video on presenting a case.

Appraisal notices go in the mail in mid-April, and protests can be emailed to protest@victoriacad.org. A review board order that still looks wrong can be taken to court, binding arbitration or the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

Payment is possible at a county tax office, by mail, by phone or online. The office takes partial payments, but penalty and interest begin on whatever is left after January 31.

  • At the counter: cash, check, money order, or a debit or credit card, with a convenience fee on cards.
  • By phone at 877-253-4085, for Victoria County accounts only. The card fee is 2.30% with a $1 minimum, and an electronic check costs a flat $0.50.
  • By mail: write the account number and the words "partial payment" on a partial payment.
  • A returned check carries a $30 service charge.

Seniors and disabled homeowners can ask about the four-installment option.

The lien securing each year's tax arrives on January 1 and stays with the house, which is why closing agents pay the year's tax from the seller's funds. New buyers should check their closing papers, because the title company may have collected from the seller and credited the buyer.

Whoever owned on January 1 stays liable for that year's tax after a sale. Delinquent tax blocks clear title, so a late Victoria account gets paid off from the proceeds. Before listing, get a balance for every unit from the tax office.

A buyer who closes mid-year may qualify for the exemption on the rest of that tax year when the seller never held it.

A cash sale does not change any of this, but it can shorten the wait. With no lender to approve an appraisal, closing depends mostly on the title search and the payoff figures, so ask the tax office for them early and give them to the title company.

A few calls, made in order, keep a Victoria sale from stalling over the tax account.

Selling a Victoria house is easier when the paperwork is lined up before the first offer. Buyers and title companies ask the same few questions, and short, documented answers keep the closing date firm.

  1. Ask the Victoria County Tax Office for the balance owed to every taxing unit on the account.
  2. Ask the appraisal district whether a homestead exemption is on file and whether any protest is still open.
  3. Find your latest statement and confirm the owner name matches your deed.
  4. Give the title company the payoff figures so it can set the closing date.
  5. Keep copies of the paid receipts, which help if a buyer or lender asks later.

faqs.q: Is the 2026 Victoria city tax rate final?
faqs.a: For 2026 the city proposed $0.4538 per $100. Confirm the final figure on your statement or with the tax office at (361) 576-3671.

faqs.q: When does Victoria property tax become delinquent?
faqs.a: February 1. A payment postmarked by January 31 counts as on time. After that the 6% penalty and 1% interest begin, and the penalty keeps growing each month until it tops out at 12% on July 1.

faqs.q: Which Victoria office changes my value or exemption?
faqs.a: The Victoria Central Appraisal District, at (361) 576-3621. The county tax office sends bills, but the appraisal district makes every change to values, exemptions and account details.

faqs.q: Can I pay only part of my Victoria tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. The county tax office takes partial payments, but whatever remains after January 31 starts to accrue penalty and interest. Put the account number and the words partial payment on the check.

faqs.q: Does a Victoria buyer owe the seller's unpaid tax?
faqs.a: Unpaid tax stays with the house until it is cleared. New owners should read their closing papers to see who paid.
